body.text: Victorian Labor MPs conduct a 'pre-mortem' in political death spiral
They say history is written by the victors, but a deflated Labor Party, a week out from election day, is already in the throes of trying to write its own version.
Ben Carroll is in an unenviable position.
The party's popularity after nearly 12 years in office has collapsed; Carroll has inherited a budget weighed down by soaring debt and a high crime rate, which is only slowly turning around.
And he must go out every day to fight an election where voters have already thumbed their nose at Labor.
With public and private polling showing Labor will lose the election, Labor MPs, past and present, are already beginning to conduct a post-(pre)-mortem.
Some of the questions posed include: Was it the right decision to knife Jacinta Allan? Was it a good idea to call a royal commission? Is the campaign hitting the right issues?
Why isn't Labor campaigning on its achievements since 2014?
Rather than focusing on the last week of campaigning, this is what is occupying Labor folk, which tells you everything you need to know about how they see their chances on November 28.
"It's an absolute disaster, it's terrible to watch,"
one senior Labor figure said.
Much of the briefing and venting is about trying to secure or sabotage the legacy of the three Labor premiers: Ben Carroll, Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews.
"It is evident that the leadership change was a disaster, and that the premier and deputy are not up to the job,'' a former minister said.
"The change has damaged our government's brand at the worst possible time — four months out from the election."

A common criticism is that the new regime had no plan beyond changing leader, and that too much of the policy agenda has been to agree with the Coalition's rhetoric rather than highlighting the achievements of the last 12 years.
Insiders say there was a months-long strategy leading up to the election, which was quickly lost.
"[Voters] aren't fools. They can know and agree that we did many great things over 12 years, and still be critical of some aspects of our government,'' the former minister said.
"For some voters, it's enough to keep them voting for Labor because you've stood by what you've delivered, and what you'll deliver in the future.
"But if you don't campaign on it, you throw away your greatest strength of incumbency."
Legacy of leaders past looms over Labor
Despite retreating from public life, Daniel Andrews remains a giant figure in Labor, and his spectre hangs over the campaign.
He led the government for nine of the past 12 years. It was Labor's most successful period.
He won three elections, increasing his majority in each one.
"There is a reason the Liberals' campaign is all about tying Ben to Jacinta and Daniel: voters f****** hate them,'' a senior ally of Carroll said.
Andrews instigated the Big Build and oversaw the massive spending that has contributed to Victoria's $173 billion net debt — a chunk of this due to COVID spending.
But he also was the lockdown premier, and some of the lingering frustration about this is washing through the electorate.
Those loyal to Andrews are placing the likely defeat at the feet of Carroll and those who led the coup; they ask what the plan was once Jacinta Allan was defeated.
Those in Carroll's camp bristle at this.
"If Jacinta was premier there would be no campaign — she wasn't even able to walk the streets of her own town, let alone in marginal electorates
'' a campaign source said.

Those on team Carroll are infuriated that Labor internal critics do not even have the "decency" to wait until the campaign is over before "white-anting the movement into thinking it was unicorns and roses when she was in charge".

"In a few months' time, Jacinta Allan and her advisors will be in the box answering questions about what they knew and when. If I were these anonymous sources, I don't think I would be tying my mast to [Allan]," a source said.

The issue that sealed Allan's fate was her steadfast resistance to calling any type of inquiry into the construction corruption allegations — an issue that would have overshadowed any attempt to press on with Labor's agenda.
We will never know if Labor would have done better under Jacinta Allan at this election, but under Ben Carroll, Labor's position has gotten worse.
The party is losing votes to the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens.
The Coalition is set to win government with a historically low primary vote under 40.

A gripe for those Carroll critics is that the political message Labor has trotted out about a possible minority Liberal-One Nation government has, in fact, pushed voters wanting a change of government straight into the hands of the Liberals.
"The best campaign in history could not escape the baggage of this government,"
one Carroll backer said.
The Labor campaign machine, so fearsome for years, has never really got going.

All of the infighting is taking focus off the Coalition, who still have big questions to answer about costings and how it proposes to keep the lights on, amid dire warnings their energy plans will worsen already shaky power security.
Liberal leader Jess Wilson is still yet to release the Coalition's costings. Economists keep asking how the Coalition is going to meet its targets.
Wilson says the costings are coming, but millions of Victorians will have voted before that happens.
On Friday, Carroll stood alongside his political mentor Steve Bracks, a man who also won three elections for Labor.
He had no problem complimenting Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, while conceding their governments made mistakes — he said all governments do.
Bracks scored an upset win in 1999 when, a week out from election day, no one gave him a chance of knocking off the dominant Jeff Kennett.
But he did, and he said Ben Carroll could repeat history.
However, the fact Labor is now caught up in venting and reprisals, rather than taking on their opponents, shows that might be very wishful thinking.
